column3: A parallel Iblis account: he refuses to be with those who prostrate.
Deniers are compelled to acknowledge the truth before tasting the consequence of their denial.
It frames disbelief as rejecting God's signs despite direct witness.
Near-exact parallel of Iblis's refusal, pride, and inclusion among the disbelievers.
The immediate continuation asks Iblis whether pride prevented his prostration.
The assurance that good deeds are not denied supplies only a reverse sense of kufr.
It explicitly joins rejecting signs, arrogance, and being among the disbelievers.
The immediate continuation gives Iblis's self-exalting comparison as the reason for refusal.
God's true loftiness contrasts only broadly with Iblis's false self-elevation.
It shows Iblis's initial stance expanding into followers, except for believers.
It connects wrongful earthly arrogance with abasement and punishment.
It places disbelief after God's creative signs, framing a refusal of evident lordship.
A parallel account identifies Iblis's departure from his Lord's command and his enmity.
The immediate consequence of Iblis's rebellion is expulsion and rejection.
God's greater good pleasure offers a distant contrast to self-claimed greatness.
A parallel prostration account isolates Iblis as the one absent from the prostrators.
Iblis's vow to lead all astray develops the focus's rebellion into its wider project.
The greater scale of divine creation rebukes the self-important comparison behind Iblis's claim.
Its command to strive against deniers does not develop Iblis's pride or refusal.
The challenge to deniers' claimed superiority parallels Iblis's claim to be better.
Its rejected route supplies no positive clarification of pride, refusal, or Iblis.
It assigns a difficult Day to deniers, extending the consequence of belonging among them.
The immediate continuation fixes the curse upon Iblis until the Day of Judgment.
Those who had been arrogant are shown sharing the same punishment with everyone else.
The warning not to be with disbelievers gives only a broad membership parallel.
The dispute narrative does not clarify Iblis's refusal, pride, or disbelief.
Its rejected route does not positively develop the focus's account of Iblis.
The arrogant explicitly declare their disbelief in the message believed by others.
Pharaoh's denial and disobedience provide a compact parallel of defiant refusal.
Its rejected route offers no positive support for the focus relation.
Recited signs are met with arrogance, after which the people are named criminals.
The same surah shows disbelievers dismissing the warner as a lying magician.
Mutual alliance among disbelievers does not clarify Iblis's personal refusal.
The rule about public evil speech is unrelated to pride and prostration.
Turning away and disbelief culminate in the greatest punishment.
The great divine bounty supplies only a distant contrast to proud self-magnification.
Human ingratitude after rescue is a broad disbelief parallel without the pride motif.
The objection to divine oneness does not clarify Iblis's prostration refusal.
Disbelief after stated limits gives a general pattern of rejecting divine command.
The gathered forces of Iblis extend the focus toward his collective following.
A high garden does not clarify Iblis's pride or exclusion.
The promise not to deny a believer's effort uses kufran in a reverse, unrelated sense.
Abraham's prayer for his father does not develop the focus's event.
Garden hospitality in the same surah does not clarify Iblis's rebellion.
Persistent arrogance after hearing God's signs closely matches defiant rejection of a known command.
Satan is explicitly described as ungrateful toward his Lord.
The invitation to purification contrasts with Pharaoh's later defiant rejection.
It assigns all true majesty to God, directly correcting self-ascribed greatness.
The parallel account immediately questions Iblis's absence from the prostrators.
The immediately preceding ayah establishes the unanimous prostration from which Iblis alone stands apart.
Punishment of disbelievers supplies only a general consequence parallel.
A parallel account directly states that Iblis refused the prostration command.
The great sign shown to Pharaoh supplies the known evidence that his following denial rejects.
Repeated rejection ends in Hell enclosing the disbelievers, a broader consequence parallel.
Pharaoh is characterized as lofty and excessive, closely paralleling arrogant rebellion.
The same-surah description places disbelief within pride and deep opposition.
Escalating signs and punishment give a broad evidentiary context but not Iblis's refusal.
Turning away and disbelieving form the same defiant movement named in the focus.
Ingratitude for divine gifts is a general disbelief parallel without pride or prostration.
The disbelievers' rushing attention does not materially clarify their arrogant refusal.
The parallel Iblis narrative continues with the respite granted after his rejection.
It completes the Iblis account by assigning Hell to him and those who follow him.
The same-surah passage links disbelieving assumptions about creation to the Fire.
A parallel account preserves Iblis's objection to prostrating before one made from clay.
Uninterrupted garden provision does not clarify pride, refusal, or disbelief.
A great scheme that misleads many echoes the extension of Iblis's rebellion into deception.
The exceptional exclusion from a saved group only structurally echoes Iblis's exception.
Paired kinds of punishment do not clarify the focus's account of Iblis.
Deniers acknowledge the truth only when confronted with punishment for their disbelief.
The Day is explicitly difficult for disbelievers, extending the focus's final classification.
Deniers are commanded toward the reality they had denied, a consequence of rejection.
The great reward for unseen reverence offers a distant contrast to Iblis's defiance.
Disbelief is made the denier's own burden and is said to increase loss and divine displeasure.
The chiefs' defense of their gods does not clarify Iblis's refusal to prostrate.
The request for doubled punishment addresses leaders whose error also led others astray.
Arrogance is explicitly the response when people are called to God's oneness.
Insatiable desire for increase provides a secondary portrait of self-expanding defiance.
It contrasts the severe punishment of disbelievers with forgiveness and great reward for believers.
The direct address to disbelievers adds little beyond the shared classification.
The same-surah distinction between righteous and corrupt people does not explain Iblis's act.
The stubborn, persistent denier is commanded into Hell, specifying the fate of such rejection.
The legal travel-prayer warning about hostile disbelievers is unrelated to the focus event.
Deniers later wish they had submitted, underscoring the irreversible cost of rejection.
The everlasting path of Hell develops the consequence attached to disbelief.
Refusal to believe in God and His messenger is assigned a prepared blazing fire.
The rule concerning alliance does not clarify Iblis's pride or prostration.
The command to magnify the Lord directly counters the self-magnification in the focus.
It explicitly joins disbelief in revelation with arrogance despite confirming witness.
It describes disbelievers as unreceptive to warning, a broad result of entrenched rejection.
Deniers admit that clear messengers came, yet their plea is declared lost.
They recognize God's favor and then deny it, making disbelief a conscious refusal.
The closing divine attributes do not clarify Iblis's refusal or its consequence.
Testing whether a report is true does not develop pride or disbelief.
Disbelievers are assigned garments of fire, a vivid consequence of their opposition to their Lord.
Mocking God's signs and worldly deception explain the irreversible punishment of deniers.
The greatest seizure is a broad punishment parallel without the focus's pride or refusal.
Enjoyment of blessings does not clarify Iblis's rebellion.
Deniers remain fixed in their position until clear evidence comes to them.
The lack of nourishment does not clarify Iblis's pride or disbelief.
Seeing the greatest sign offers only a distant contrast to refusing a known divine command.
It explicitly joins scorning God's worship with arrogance and its resulting punishment.
Arrogance toward God's signs is named as the cause of humiliating punishment.
God asks what prevented Iblis from prostrating; Iblis answers with his claim to be better.
Iblis is ordered down because arrogance has no place there, and is made one of the humiliated.
Iblis's request for reprieve continues the immediate consequence of his proud refusal.
The granted reprieve continues the parallel Iblis narrative after his exclusion.
Iblis turns his refusal into a vow to obstruct people from God's straight path.
His vow to approach people from every direction develops the focus into an active program of misguidance.
The expulsion and promised filling of Hell with Iblis and his followers complete the judgment sequence.
Those who deny God's signs and are arrogant about them are named companions of the Fire.
Denial of God's signs joined with arrogance bars entry to Paradise and leads to punishment.
Arrogant leaders challenge the faith of those who accept the messenger, immediately framing the response at 7:76.
Arrogance without right causes people to turn from every divine sign even when they see it.
Pharaoh and his chiefs receive signs yet act arrogantly as a criminal people.
Iblis explicitly says he will not prostrate to a human made from sounding clay.
The parallel account immediately orders Iblis out after his refusal.
It places the divine curse on Iblis until the Day of Judgment.
Iblis's request for reprieve follows directly from his expulsion.
The appointed known time completes the reprieve detail but adds little to the refusal itself.
Iblis vows to make wrongdoing attractive and mislead humanity after his exclusion.
His stated exception for God's sincere servants marks the limit of his intended counter-community.
God declares the straight path that stands over against Iblis's pledged obstruction.
God denies Iblis authority over His servants, except those who choose to follow him.
Hell is named as the promised destination for Iblis's followers.
Disbelief in the Hereafter is linked to hearts that reject and to arrogance.
God's knowledge of the hidden and open is followed by the declaration that He does not love the arrogant.
The arrogant are commanded to enter Hell's gates for an everlasting abode.
Iblis objects to Adam's honor and threatens to seize Adam's descendants, extending his self-superiority claim.
Iblis and those who follow him are assigned Hell as a full recompense.
Iblis is permitted to entice and recruit others, developing the focus's rebellion into collective misguidance.
God limits Iblis's authority while excepting those who choose to follow him.
Pharaoh's transgression gives a broad exemplar of defiant opposition to divine command.
Pharaoh is shown God's signs in full before he denies and refuses them.
His accusation of Moses shows resistance to a sign through hostile reinterpretation.
Iblis is identified as an enemy to Adam and his wife, giving the human consequence of the refusal narrative.
A people are said to act arrogantly toward their messengers after receiving their call.
The opponents are described as arrogant toward the message and forsaking it in nightly talk.
Those who reject the meeting with God demand extraordinary proof because they have become greatly arrogant.
They deny the signs despite inward certainty, doing so out of wrongdoing and arrogance.
Pharaoh's exclusive claim to authority shows a ruler's self-exalting rejection of divine lordship.
Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly without right and deny their return to God.
Qarun, Pharaoh, and Haman act arrogantly despite clear proofs from Moses.
Believers fall in prostration when reminded of God's signs and do not act arrogantly, the direct inverse of the focus.
Arrogance on earth and evil plotting are condemned, with the plot returning upon its authors.
Those who lie about God have blackened faces on the Day of Judgment; Hell is named the abode of the arrogant.
The arrogant are commanded to enter Hell through its gates for an everlasting abode.
Moses seeks refuge from every arrogant person who does not believe in the Day of Account.
Arguing against God's signs without authority is tied to pride that God seals within the arrogant heart.
Those who dispute God's signs act from a pride they can never attain.
Those too arrogant to worship God are assigned entry into Hell in humiliation.
'Aad claim superior strength in arrogant rejection, and the verse directly corrects their comparison with God's greater power.
Pharaoh's display of dominion and rivers models public self-exaltation before his later claim of superiority.
Pharaoh asks whether he is better than a weaker opponent, closely paralleling Iblis's self-superior comparison.
After learning God's signs, the denier takes them in mockery and is promised humiliating punishment.
The disbelievers' arrogance is explicitly called the arrogance of ignorance and contrasted with God-sent tranquility.
The subject turns away and acts arrogantly after considering the warning, a direct pride-and-refusal parallel.
Pharaoh turns his back and strives in opposition after his denial and disobedience.
Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord is an explicit instance of extreme self-exaltation.
